title: Coverage Summary
intro: 228 names under coverage, classified on two axes. Axis 1 is business durability — how likely the business is to become useless (reviewed per ticker by the daily classification routine: durable franchise, cyclical, AI-exposed, structurally challenged, turnaround, special situation). Axis 2 is price — downside room and asymmetry from the model's own numbers (Ratio B, distance to the EPP panic floor, adjusted-vs-market composite, conservative 2-yr case). Today: 36 compounders at a low price, 6 in the AI-fear basket, 40 quality names neutrally valued, 49 priced for perfection, 46 with too much cycle risk, 26 cyclicals at a fair or discounted price, and 25 structural, turnaround or special situations. Everything below is a model output, not a price target. Taxonomy change today: software and IT-services names with a live generative-AI substitution debate (Adobe, ServiceNow, SAP, Wolters Kluwer, Intuit, Accenture, Salesforce, IBM, Alphabet, Uber) now carry their own AI-EXPOSED durability class instead of being filed under 'durable'. That is why the compounder list shrank and the AI-fear basket appeared — the price rules did not change.

sections.heading: Best buys — durable businesses with limited downside
body: Downside limited by the model's own floor and asymmetry, AND low-to-neutral risk of the business becoming useless. Ranked by a blend of model-vs-market gap, Ratio B, conservative 2-yr return, distance to floor and obsolescence risk. Buys at today's prices, not on a further pullback.

items.x: Oracle tops the ranking on mechanics: the stock sits within 2% of the model's own $144 BEAR scenario after the BBB- downgrade scare, so Ratio B rounds to zero and the model-vs-market gap is +1.94. The franchise (database + OCI, $30B+ of new AI cloud contracts) is durable; the risk is financing — $40B of debt plus a $20B equity raise this fiscal year. Buy, but size it as an AI-capex bet, not a bond proxy.
Stryker 1.5% above its EPP floor with 0.22x Ratio B and a +1.11 gap — a medtech compounder at the floor is the cleanest quality-at-a-low-price setup in the book.
T-Mobile: still the best combination of durability and asymmetry — 0.30x Ratio B, +1.49 gap, 96% upside to bull versus 29% downside. Capital-intensive oligopoly, nothing here becomes useless.
Home Depot at 0.15x Ratio B, 7% above floor, conservative 2-yr +34%. A frozen housing market is a trough for a durable franchise, not a broken one.
Marsh McLennan 7% above floor at 0.22x Ratio B; the CEO transition (Matt Stadler, Sept 16) is worth watching but the fee-based moat and 19-year margin streak are intact.
PSEG pushed toward a 52-week low on rate sensitivity — now 0.5% above its floor with 0.33x Ratio B and guidance reaffirmed. Regulated wires plus nuclear; obsolescence risk as low as equities get.
S&P Global 11.5% BELOW its own panic floor at 0.20x Ratio B — a ratings duopoly plus index flywheel below the floor. Buy on safety first, upside second.
KKR: +1.01 gap, 0.43x Ratio B, conservative 2-yr +17%. Fee-related earnings durable, realizations cyclical — size below MRSH and SPGI.
AutoZone 13% above floor at 0.20x Ratio B into the Sept 22 print. Counter-cyclical buyback compounder; the EV mix headwind is decade-scale.
Waste Management at 0.40x Ratio B, +0.93 gap; landfill moat with pricing power. The floor distance (+75%) is the only thing keeping it out of the top five.

sections.heading: The AI-fear basket — cheap because the market is pricing disruption
body: Franchises with a live generative-AI substitution debate (software, IT services, information, search, mobility). Kept OUT of the compounder list on purpose: the discount is real and the reported numbers keep refusing the bear case, but this is the one group where 'becoming useless' is a non-zero scenario. Own as a basket, sized as one position, not as single convictions.

items.x: Adobe 7.5% BELOW its floor at 0.23x Ratio B after a beat-and-raise (AI-first ARR $650M) — the market's clearest 'generative-AI loser' bet. The numbers keep refusing it; the CEO transition (Dec 1) is the next test. Core of the basket.
SAP: +0.94 gap, 0.68x Ratio B; the system-of-record is sticky, the debate is whether the Joule agent layer ships (17 of 200 agents delivered). Lower AI risk than the rest of the basket.
ServiceNow at $136 after the software-sector selloff: 0.43x Ratio B, +0.59 gap, 102% upside to bull. Per-seat licensing versus agentic AI is unresolved — the purest expression of the fear.
Wolters Kluwer 16% above floor at 0.68x Ratio B; renewal numbers keep refusing the AI-disruption thesis. Information services are where substitution is most plausible, so it stays in the basket.
Intuit 10% above floor, 0.48x Ratio B, conservative 2-yr +37%, but the composite reads fairly valued and AI tax-prep is a direct substitute for TurboTax. In the basket on price, not on conviction.

Accenture: 0.45x Ratio B, fairly valued composite, Guggenheim downgrade on weak organic growth and falling job listings. GenAI deflates IT-services pricing and Accenture is also the delivery partner for it — both sides of the trade in one name.

sections.heading: Main dangers across the book
body: Crowding at highs. 49 quality names and 46 cyclicals are priced for perfection or at a cycle peak — 42% of coverage. The largest single risk remains buying good companies at the top of their ranges.

The AI trade, both sides. The AI-fear basket (ADBE, NOW, SAP, WKL, INTU, ACN) and the AI-capex winners (NVDA, AMD, MRVL, AVGO, PLTR, VST, CEG, TT, ETN) are mirror images of one debate. A capex digestion phase hits them in opposite directions; a software-sector selloff like this week's hits the basket regardless of the numbers.
Cheap-for-a-reason. Cable (CMCSA, CHTR), California utilities (EIX, PCG), Fiserv and Nike screen cheapest in coverage; in every case the E in the floor is contested. They are labelled, not promoted.

Rate sensitivity on the buy side. PEG, SCHW, TMUS and the regulated names on the buy list all lose if long rates keep rising; the EU banks on the sell list lose if they fall. The book is not neutral to the rate path.
